document.title: U.S. Engagement with the Taliban on Usama Bin Laden
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Taliban File Update
document.note: [Secret] Newly declassified State Department summary (SECRET NODIS, circa July 16, 2001) of U.S. efforts to press the Taliban to expel Usama bin Laden. It records over 30 approaches between 1996 and summer 2001, only three of them in the first year of the Bush administration. After the August 1998 embassy bombings Mullah Omar phoned State Department officials and expressed interest in a confidential dialogue. The U.S. warned that harboring bin Laden hurt Afghanistan's prospects and that the Taliban would be held accountable for attacks. The U.S. knew of the militant training camps' locations from 1997. In October 1999 the Taliban suggested a trial by Islamic scholars or monitoring by the OIC or UN.

key_claims: Since 1996 the US treated bin Laden and terrorism as the preeminent issue with the Taliban, predating the 1998 embassy bombings.
Taliban officials repeatedly claimed UBL was 'restricted', denied his fatwas, and said no evidence existed against him.
The Taliban refused to expel UBL, citing hospitality rules, lack of an extradition treaty, and that expulsion would topple the Taliban.
In October 1999 the Taliban proposed supervision by OIC/NAM/UN or a panel of Islamic scholars; the US rejected the first as not meeting UNSCR 1267.
The Taliban offered then withdrew a US visit to militant training camps in eastern Afghanistan in 1997.
After the August 1998 bombings and US strikes on Khost, Mullah Omar briefly signaled interest in confidential dialogue, but talks remained fruitless through July 2001.
